title: Sonia Gandhi says 'many elections have been stolen'; BJP points to the Emergency
dek: In an interview before her memoir's release, the Congress leader said 12 years of BJP rule had done 'great damage' to India's democracy and institutions. Law Minister Arjun Ram Meghwal told her to remember the Emergency.
body:
Congress Parliamentary Party chairperson Sonia Gandhi has said that "great damage has been done to the fabric of our country, our democracy and our institutions" in the 12 years of Prime Minister Narendra Modi's government, and that "many elections have been stolen". The BJP hit back, with Union Law Minister Arjun Ram Meghwal telling her to remember the Emergency.

Mrs Gandhi made the remarks in a newspaper interview published on Saturday, ahead of the release on 10 November of her memoir, Belonging: A Journey of Love.

## What she said

Mrs Gandhi said restoring the country's systems "to health" would take time and great effort from political parties even after the present government leaves office, but that she was "optimistic" that people would welcome "a return to proper governance", according to reports of the interview.

She said the opposition did not compete on a level field, citing what she called the government's "complete stranglehold" on institutions, "especially the Election Commission", its control of mainstream media, its money power and its "exploitation of religion". It had been "amply proved in recent months that many elections have been stolen, and people are now more aware of it", she said. She did not name specific elections, according to the reports.

Asked what the Congress could learn from Mr Modi's rise, she said he came from a very different ideological background and "I don't think we have much to learn from the RSS". She said she had never wondered how things would have gone had she become prime minister in 2004, and described the UPA years, when Manmohan Singh led the government and she led the party, as largely positive. She also said democratic rights were curtailed during the Emergency of 1975-77, according to one report.

## The response

Mr Meghwal said Mrs Gandhi "ought to remember that era as well", referring to the Emergency, when thousands of opposition leaders were jailed and the press was censored, according to reports. He cited Mr Modi's description of India as "the mother of democracy".

BJP spokesperson Pradeep Bhandari said in a post on X that the NDA's rate of election wins was lower under the present Chief Election Commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar, than under V.S. Sampath, who held the post from 2012 to 2015 during UPA rule. He put the figures at about 66% and 75% respectively, and asked whether Mrs Gandhi had been doing "vote chori" (vote theft) for the BJP, the phrase Rahul Gandhi uses for his allegations. The Election Commission has not responded to her remarks; it has rejected the opposition's allegations of manipulation in the past.

## Background

The Congress has demanded Mr Kumar's resignation, accusing him of acting at the government's behest, and the INDIA bloc has held protests over alleged electoral malpractice, including a rally at Delhi's Ramlila Maidan on 1 November. The dispute has sharpened during the Election Commission's special intensive revision (SIR) of voter rolls; Home Minister Amit Shah has offered a special session of Parliament to debate it if the Congress writes to the Prime Minister.

The memoir, which runs to 544 pages and is published by HarperCollins India, traces Mrs Gandhi's life from her childhood in Italy's Veneto region to meeting Rajiv Gandhi in Cambridge, her arrival in India and the assassinations of Indira Gandhi in 1984 and Rajiv Gandhi in 1991, according to reports. Penguin Random House India, which had acquired the book, withdrew as its Indian publisher after disagreements over the manuscript. Some Congress leaders alleged that the publisher had come under pressure to remove passages about Mr Modi, the RSS and China; the publisher denied any outside pressure and declined to explain the disagreement, citing confidentiality.
